## Psalm 143 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Background / Title

Psalm 143 is the seventh and last of the seven Penitential Psalms (with Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130). In the early church they were sung on Ash Wednesday. Martin Luther called Psalm 143 one of the “Pauline Psalms” because v. 2 anticipates Paul’s theology in Romans 3. Pope Innocent III (1198–1216) ordered all seven penitential psalms prayed daily during Lent. In the medieval scheme, Psalm 143 was directed against the sin of sloth. — enduringword.com; 1517.org (via search excerpt); Spurgeon, archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php

Opinions on authorship and date differ: traditional commentators (Gill, Spurgeon, Kretzmann) accept the Davidic superscription and often link the psalm to Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 12:9). Ellicott thinks the psalm is post-exilic because “hardly a phrase is not derived from some older source,” and suggests the speaker may be the personified community rather than an individual. — biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm

Spurgeon notes the psalm is “rather a vindication of his own integrity, and an indignant prayer against his slanderers, than a confession of fault.” He suspects “seven penitentials were needed by ecclesiastical rabbis, and therefore this was impressed into the service.” — archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php

---

### v. 1: *“O LORD, hear my prayer. In Your faithfulness, give ear to my plea; in Your righteousness, answer me.”*

David opens with an urgent double cry — “hear” and “give ear” — wanting God to pay special attention. He appeals not to his own merit but to God’s **faithfulness** (His covenant-keeping character) and **righteousness** (His commitment to do what is right). Gill: “he does not plead his own faith… but the faithfulness of God to his promises.” Ellicott agrees: “‘Faithfulness’ recalls the covenant promise, ‘righteousness’ the faith… that the Judge of all the world must do right,” comparing 1 John 1:9. Spurgeon: “Even the sterner attributes of God are upon the side of the man who humbly trusts.” — biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm; archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php

---

### v. 2: *“Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You.”*

This is the most theologically significant verse of the psalm. David does not ask for a trial before God’s justice; he knows he cannot stand on his own righteousness. Gill: “in a legal sense… no man living [shall] be justified… by the deeds of the law, as the apostle explains it, Romans 3:20.” Spurgeon: “David told out the doctrine of universal condemnation by the law long before Paul had taken his pen to write the same truth.” This verse is why Luther classified Psalm 143 as a “Pauline Psalm.” David appeals as “Your servant” — a relationship, not a claim of innocence. — enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm; archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php

Ellicott sees here “the apparent paradox of the Book of Job” — man appeals to God’s justice for vindication before men, but instantly recoils, knowing before God none can stand. — biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm

**Tradition note — Lutheran:** Kretzmann’s Popular Commentary (Lutheran) stresses that “not one human being can stand before God in his own righteousness… It is only by realizing and acknowledging his sinfulness without reserve and throwing himself entirely upon the mercy of the Lord that any person can expect justification, namely, by means of the righteousness of Christ imputed to him.” — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/psalms-143.html (via search excerpt)

**Tradition note — Reformed/Piper:** John Piper, preaching from this psalm at Desiring God, notes the surprising fact that David does not first flee to God’s mercy but to God’s righteousness. If righteousness meant strict distributive justice, David the sinner would be crushed. But David understands God’s righteousness as His commitment to uphold the honor of His own name by saving those who trust in Him. Piper calls this “the crucial link” — God’s honor is at stake in David’s deliverance. — desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-argue-with-god (via search excerpt)

---

### v. 3: *“For the enemy has pursued my soul, crushing my life to the ground, making me dwell in darkness like those long since dead.”*

David’s enemy has hunted him down and crushed him — not just physically but in his *soul*. Gill notes “darkness” may mean literal cave-dwelling (as from Saul) or “great affliction of body and mind, frequently signified by darkness.” Ellicott notes the phrase “made me to dwell in darkness” is verbally identical to Lamentations 3:6. “Long dead” is literally “dead of old” or “dead for ever” (LXX: *nekrous aiōnos*). — biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm

The significant “For” beginning the verse shows that David accepts the enemy’s attacks as, in some sense, God’s chastening — the affliction is evidence that God is visiting for sin. — Ellicott; Expositor’s Bible (Maclaren), biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/143.htm

---

### v. 4: *“My spirit grows faint within me; my heart is dismayed inside me.”*

David describes the inward effect: his spirit is “overwhelmed” (wrapped or covered over with grief) and his heart is “desolate” or “astonished” (stunned, like one struck numb). Spurgeon: “David was no stoic: he felt his banishment, and smarted under the cruel assaults… He felt perplexed and overturned, lonely and afflicted.” Spurgeon also notes that “such words our Lord Jesus might have used” — connecting this to Christ’s agony in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:38). Enduring Word makes the same point: “In Gethsemane, before His betrayal and crucifixion, Jesus said: *My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death*.” — archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php; enduringword.com

---

### vv. 5–6: *“I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Your works; I consider the work of Your hands. I stretch out my hands to You; my soul thirsts for You like a parched land. Selah.”*

David refuses to drown in despair. He deliberately turns his thoughts: **memory → meditation → musing**. Spurgeon calls these “the three graces, ministering grace to a mind depressed.” He remembers not primarily his own past but God’s past works — creation, covenant, rescue. Enduring Word: “David didn’t remember his past as much as he remembered the LORD’s past works.”

The posture of stretched-out hands is one of desperate supplication. “My soul thirsts for You like a parched land” echoes Psalm 63:1; the image is of cracked ground gaping open for rain. Spurgeon: “As the soil cracks, and yawns, and thus opens its mouth in dumb pleadings, so did the Psalmist’s soul break with longings.” — enduringword.com; archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php

The **Selah** marks the halfway point. The Expositor’s Bible notes this is unusual — Selah is not found in Books 4 and 5 of the Psalter except here and Psalm 140. — biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/143.htm

---

### v. 7: *“Answer me quickly, O LORD; my spirit fails. Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.”*

The second half (vv. 7–12) is pure petition. David’s spirit is at the edge of collapse, so he pleads for speed. “Hide not Your face” is a standing petition in the Psalms (e.g., 27:9; 102:2). To lose the sense of God’s favour is, for David, equivalent to death — “like those who go down into the pit” (the grave, or Sheol). Gill: “for as in the favour of God is life, his absence is as death.” — biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm

---

### v. 8: *“Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, for I have put my trust in You. Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.”*

David asks for two things: (1) to **hear** God’s *hesed* (lovingkindness / covenant love) at daybreak, and (2) to **know** the way he should walk. “In the morning” may mean literally early, or figuratively the dawn of hope after the night of weeping. Ellicott: “The expression either means ‘early,’ or is figurative of the dawn of hope and salvation.” Enduring Word notes that *hesed* has been understood for centuries as mercy, kindness, and love — not merely “covenant loyalty.”

David’s pleas are: “for in You do I trust” and “for to You I lift up my soul.” Spurgeon: “If the soul will not rise of itself we must lift it, lift it up unto God.” The logic: “surely the God to whom we endeavour to lift up our soul will condescend to show us what he would have us to do.” — enduringword.com; archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm

---

### v. 9: *“Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge.”*

A direct prayer for deliverance. The Hebrew phrase “I flee to You to hide me” is literally “unto Thee have I hidden [myself].” Ellicott explains it as a pregnant construction: “to Thee I have fled and hid myself.” Gill renders it “with thee have I hid” — he disclosed his troubles to God alone. Enduring Word: “David would not take shelter in sinful pleasures, in the distractions of entertainment, in positive thinking, in self-reliance, in bitterness, or in vengeance. David was determined to take shelter in the LORD.” — biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm; enduringword.com

---

### v. 10: *“Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God. May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.”*

This is one of the richest verses in the psalm. David does not pray “cause me to do Your will” but “**teach** me to do Your will” — God instructs, but the believer must willingly obey. Enduring Word: “In all his reliance upon God, he knew that God would not obey for him.”

The mention of God’s “good Spirit” (or “Thy Spirit is good”) is one of the relatively few OT references to the Holy Spirit in personal terms. Gill: “the Holy Spirit of God is meant, the third Person in the Trinity; who is ‘good’ essentially… and effectively is the author of the good work of grace upon the heart.” Enduring Word connects this to the New Covenant outpouring and cites Cyril of Alexandria (4th–5th c.): “Cyril gathereth from this text, that the good Spirit is God, because none is good but God.”

**“Land of uprightness” or “level ground”?** Ellicott translates “level land” (as in Deuteronomy 4:43, “plain country”) used metaphorically for tranquility and safety. Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran) agree: “lead him in a level country… The geographical term *’eretz mîshôr*… is here applied spiritually.” Gill sees it as “the land where only truly righteous and upright persons dwell” — ultimately heaven. — enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm; studylight.org excerpt from Keil & Delitzsch

---

### v. 11: *“For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me. In Your righteousness, bring my soul out of trouble.”*

David prays for revival — renewal of life and vitality — not for his own benefit, but “for Your name’s sake.” Enduring Word: “A genuine concern for the sake of God’s name is a necessary aspect of true revival — and not for the name or the advancement of any man or woman of God.” He also asks deliverance “in Your righteousness” — again appealing to God’s character, not his own. Gill: “for as he had his bodily troubles and other outward affliction, he had soul troubles, through the corruptions of his nature, the temptations of Satan, and the hidings of God’s face.” — enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm

---

### v. 12: *“And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies. Destroy all who afflict me, for I am Your servant.”*

This is the most debated verse, an imprecatory prayer. Spurgeon frankly admits: “We could not pray just so with our Christian light; but under Old Testament arrangements the spirit of it was congruous to the law… It is a petition which justice sanctions, but the spirit of love is not at home in presenting it.” Yet he also notes that David “was of so generous a mind, and dealt so tenderly with Saul, that he could hardly have meant all that his words are made in our version to say.”

Enduring Word places this prayer within the logic of the psalm: David “asked God to deal with his enemies; but before that, he asked God to deal with him.” The closing phrase “for I am Your servant” is David’s ultimate plea — his relationship to God. Kidner (quoted in Enduring Word): “For God is pledged to His servant as surely as His servant is pledged to Him.”

Gill notes the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic versions read these verbs in the **future tense** (“Thou shalt quicken… bring out… cut off… destroy”), making it a prophecy rather than (or as well as) a prayer. — enduringword.com; archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps143.php; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/143.htm

**Tradition differences on v. 12:** Spurgeon’s discomfort represents a common evangelical tension with imprecatory prayers. Piper (via Desiring God) addresses this by arguing that David’s prayer for destruction of enemies is tied to God’s righteousness: “There are circumstances… where there can be no deliverance without destruction, and to pray for one is also to pray for the other” (McCaw, cited on studylight.org). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary treats the verse straightforwardly as David’s petition for God to vindicate His servant, without apology. — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-143.html (via search excerpt); desiringgod.org (Piper sermon excerpt)

## Tradition-Specific Notes

### Reformed / Piper (Baptist with strong Reformed soteriology)
John Piper’s sermon “How to Argue with God” (desiringgod.org) treats Psalm 143 as a model for filling one’s mouth with arguments before God. Piper identifies three categories in David’s requests: (1) general desire to be heard, (2) desire for godliness, (3) desire for safety. He stresses that David’s appeal to God’s “righteousness” does not mean strict distributive justice but God’s commitment to uphold His own name by saving those who trust Him. Piper also emphasises that David always pairs requests for safety with requests for moral and spiritual transformation. — desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-argue-with-god (via search excerpt)

### Lutheran
Luther classified this as a “Pauline Psalm” alongside Psalms 32, 51, and 130. In his 1517 lectures on the penitential psalms (revised 1525), Luther saw the Psalter as a “little Bible” and the penitential psalms as giving believers the words to cry out to God in distress, lament sin, and confess trust in God’s righteousness alone. The 1517.org article notes Luther’s hermeneutic of law and gospel at work in these psalms: through the law comes knowledge of sin (crushing self-justification), and through the gospel comes knowledge of God’s mercy in Christ. Kretzmann’s Lutheran commentary on v. 2 explicitly ties justification to “the righteousness of Christ imputed to him.” — 1517.org (search excerpt); studylight.org Kretzmann excerpt

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
David Guzik at enduringword.com (a Calvary Chapel / charismatic-leaning ministry) reads the psalm devotionally with an emphasis on prayer life, spiritual thirst, and revival. He highlights the distinction in v. 10 between “teach me to do Your will” versus “cause me to do it” — God guides, but the believer must obey. On vv. 11–12, Guzik emphasises that true revival is sought for God’s glory, not personal advancement. His application stresses that believers should “pray as David did — appealing not to our own supposed righteousness but to God’s mercy, faithfulness, and character.”

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott treats the psalm as post-exilic and possibly communal rather than individual, noting that virtually every phrase is drawn from older psalms and prophets. He sees this not as a defect but as evidence that “the deeper religious life of the post-exile times was upheld and cherished by the experience of past times.” He reads “land of uprightness” as “level land” — metaphorical of tranquility and happiness. — biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/143.htm
